sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Later tokens are costlier to generate than earlier tokens. On frontier open weight models, the disparity in cost may rise to as much as 7x. Through frequent compaction, we show across a broad range of long-horizon and long-input tasks that frontier language models sacrifice little to no task accuracy when maintaining short contexts. We further demonstrate that LLM performance does not collapse on long-horizon software engineering tasks even when taking at most one action per context, and based on that we outline the concept of semantic state space models (SSSMs). Our findings question the need for long-context language models.

sections.content: 2026-11-4 You dont need long context Peter Belcak, Saurav Muralidharan, Jindong Jiang, Yonggan Fu, Wonmin Byeon, Hanrong Ye, Ryan Angilly, Ali Taghibakhshi, Shih-Yang Liu, Siru Ouyang, Greg Heinrich, Pavlo Molchanov Abstract. Later tokens are costlier to generate than earlier tokens. On frontier open weight models, the disparity in cost may rise to as much as 7x. Through frequent compaction, we show across broad range of long-horizon and long-input tasks that frontier language models sacrifice little to no task accuracy when maintaining short contexts. We further demonstrate that LLM performance does not collapse on long-horizon software engineering tasks even when taking at most one action per context, and based on that we outline the concept of semantic state space models (SSSMs). Our findings question the need for long-context language models. Links: Lab Project Moonshot: Local Frontier Intelligence 1. Introduction Not all tokens are generated equal. Token generation latency and memory footprint both grow with the number of tokens in language models context. This is due to the inherent linear1 relationship between the computational cost of generating token and its depth within context [25]. Figure 1 shows the cloud token generation cost as function of context window size for selection of popular open-weight models. Observe that there is considerable monetary benefit to serving models on cloud GPUs with consistently shorter contexts. This fact is often hidden from the end user since retail token prices are quoted at fixed price per 1M tokens regardless of the input context length. Note that the extent of cost reductions (3.6 to 7) rivals or exceeds that of many other orthogonal optimization methods such as aggressive quantization or structured sparsification [5, 14, 8]. Monetary cost is not the only quality of LM workloads that suffers when inputs are long. Figure 1 The cost of long context. Dollar cost of generating 1M output tokens on an existing input KV cache as function of the context window size, obtained by converting the measured peak decode throughput of each deployment at on-demand H100 prices ($3.85 per GPU-hour, Nebius, Sept. 2026). Input request lengths are drawn uniformly at random. GLM 5.2 and Kimi K2.6 are served with INT4 weights and BF16 activations, Qwen 3 Coder Next is served in BF16. Serving at context window size of 256K rather than 16K costs 3.6 more per generated token for GLM, 5.6 more for Kimi, and 7 more for Qwen. 1Model architectures with constant cost of token generation with respect to context depth have been repeatedly proposed but have never been fully embraced linear-cost attention-based mechanisms remain the backbone of all popular language models. 2026 NVIDIA. All rights reserved. You dont need long context Figure 2 The burden of long context. The token generation latency, token throughput, and memory footprint of several open-source models measured on an NVIDIA DGX Spark plotted as function of input context length. For several models, later tokens take approximately 2x longer to generate than earlier tokens and require larger memory footprint. Figure 2 shows the token generation latency, throughput, and memory footprint of several popular locally-run coding models as function of the input context length. Observe how the generation inter-token latency approximately doubles for several models across the measured context lengths, implying doubling of the time required to generate response at longer contexts. Put simply, the longer the input context provided to the language model (LM), the slower, more memory hungry, and more expensive its output token generation. Given the considerable benefits of keeping input context short in both cloud and edge LM use, one would assume that popular LMs would have naturally evolved to operate on contexts only as short as necessary to complete their tasks. This could not be farther from the truth. As seen in Table 1, which compares the lengths of well-known works of writing with the context window sizes of representative proprietary and open-weight models, context window sizes have vastly outgrown many influential writings. It would seem that models have been evolving to accommodate the ever larger possible inputs rather than to maximize efficiency. The enormous context window sizes of contemporary LMs and the tangible cost advantages of keeping their contexts short thus appear to be at odds with each other. While operating with longer contexts might in some cases be thought beneficial to model task accuracy, we must ask: RQ0 Are long contexts necessary? If not, lets do away with long contexts and long-context models. And, if there are currently any objective benefits of keeping long context models, we can likely preserve them by making the appropriate post-training adjustments to future models. Literary works Model context window sizes Work Words Tokens Model Words Tokens 27K 48K 37K MiniMax M2.7 [31] The Old Man and the Sea [21] 64K Claude Opus 4.5 [2] The Great Gatsby [15] Quran (Saheeh Intl translation) [38] 156K 207K Gemma 4 31B [16] 181K 241K Kimi K2.6 [32] King James New Testament [26] 184K 245K Qwen 3 Coder Next [9] Great Expectations [12] 481K 640K Gemini 3.8 Flash [13] The Lord of the Rings [42] 566K 753K GLM 5.2 [51] War and Peace [43] 603K 802K GPT 5.6 Sol [34] King James Old Testament [26] 150K 150K 192K 192K 197K 750K 750K 790K 200K 200K 256K 256K 262K 1M 1M 1.05M Table 1 Lengths of literary works against model context window sizes. Word counts use the cited English editions. Word-token conversions use approximately 1.33 tokens per English word, while actual counts vary with text and tokenizer. Models and their context window sizes are detailed in Section 2.3. 2 You dont need long context To answer RQ0, look at where the so-called long contexts (and, correspondingly, large context windows) in language modeling come from. Broadly, there are two types of workloads that often result in long input contexts being passed to LMs: LCW1 Workloads of long-horizon tasks tasks that may require many actions in order to be completed and where the context builds up as the model makes its way towards the completion of the task [11, 47, 52]. LCW2 Workloads of long-input tasks tasks that require operating across large amount of input information [6, 45, 29]. Examining these two types of workloads more closely, it is not immediately clear whether operating on long contexts is necessary in order to complete them. In particular, the entire conversational history of LCW1 does not necessarily need to be considered at every step of long-horizon operation in order to successfully complete the task. Likewise, the long inputs of LCW2 do not necessarily need to be ingested in their entirety at all times in order for the workload to conclude successfully. Moreover, observe that the tasks in LCW2 can always be reduced to LCW1 by storing the long input as resource and equipping the LM with tool for selective input reading. Motivated by the advantages of keeping LM generation contexts short and the apparent lack of clear justification for the popular practice for ingesting long inputs all at once and maintaining long conversational histories as discussed above, we decompose RQ0 to pose the following research questions: RQ1 Can long-horizon tasks be completed without long contexts? RQ2 Can long-input tasks be completed without long contexts? RQ3 Can long-horizon tasks be completed taking no more than single action per context? The rest of this paper is aimed at curtly answering these questions. 2. Methodology We use one methodology to answer all research questions posed in Section 1. 2.1. Definitions The base term context is, unfortunately, considerably overloaded in language modelling. Below we outline our working definitions intended to fix the meaning of otherwise vaguely interpreted terms commonly used in the community and relied on throughout this paper. Their numerical boundaries are rough rules of thumb. Inference step. An inference step is one invocation of an LM to produce output. In agentic workflows, it typically coincides with one agent turn of conversation. Input context. At given inference step, the input context is the complete sequence of tokens made available to the LM to produce output. It may include system instructions, the task input, prior model outputs, tool results, and any other conversational history. Output context. At given inference step, the output context is the complete sequence of tokens generated by the LM in the inference step. It may include thinking trace, tool calls, user-oriented outputs, or other model output artifacts. Context. At given inference step, the context is the input context, the input context and an associated output context, or the input context and any token space reserved for possible output context. Context window and context window size. The context window is the space of tokens an LM can comprehend at any given point, usually imposed by the models architecture or indirectly by its post-training data bias. Contexts exceeding context windows may cause system errors or unexpected behavior. The context window size is the maximum number of tokens that an LM endpoint can process in one invocation, whether imposed by the models context window or narrowed by its serving configuration. 3 You dont need long context Long context. We call context long when its length approaches constituting significant fraction of context window size of many contemporary frontier models, which tends to rest at approximately 256K tokens or more at the time of this study. We further call an execution regime or context-management strategy long-context if it permits the context to grow toward that scale, even when an individual run terminates before reaching the context window size. Short context. We call context short when its length is much closer to zero than to the context window size common to many contemporary frontier models. In the operating regimes emphasized in this work, short contexts are commonly limited to roughly 16K50K tokens. Note that we take short to mean short relative to common context window sizes; it does not mean that the context is small in an absolute linguistic sense. Even context window sizes of 16K50K tokens suffice to contain elaborate literary works (cf. Table 1). Long-input task. long input task is task which is accompanied by long input i.e., input information that would constitute long context if ingested directly. The term long input refers to the size of the available task input, irrespective of whether harness places all of it in the model context at once or exposes it through selective input reading. Long-horizon task. long-horizon task is task whose completion requires many sequential model actions, with later actions depending on the observations, artifacts, or decisions produced by earlier ones. Absent context management, the resulting interaction history accumulates across the task and may grow toward models context window size and form long context. 2.2. Benchmarks We assess the merits of RQ1RQ3 by considering two groups of benchmarks corresponding to the sources of long context identified in Section 1: long-horizon tasks (LCW1), whose interaction histories grow as an agent acts, and long-input tasks (LCW2), whose source material can itself fill or exceed models context window size. Our ensemble of benchmarks covers realistic software-engineering, information-seeking, and tool-use workloads with controlled long-input diagnostics. Long-horizon task benchmarks. The long-horizon task benchmark group aims to represent real sequential workflows in which the model must repeatedly inspect an environment, select an action, observe its result, and use that result to decide what to do next. Without context management, every command, tool response, retrieved document, and intermediate decision is appended to an ever-growing history. The software-engineering benchmarks are particularly representative examples because repository exploration, implementation, and validation naturally form long sequences of interdependent actions. The remaining benchmarks broaden this group to information retrieval, user interaction, and cross-tool orchestration. SWE-bench Verified [23] is human-validated set of 500 real GitHub issue-resolution tasks from popular repositories, where the agent must produce patch that passes the repositorys held-out test suite. SWE-bench Multilingual [48] comprises 300 manually curated issue-resolution tasks from repositories across nine programming languages. It tests repository exploration, implementation, and validation across different language ecosystems. Terminal-Bench 2.1 [30] is an agentic benchmark of 89 real command-line tasks executed in sandboxed containers and scored by per-task verifiers, measuring end-to-end terminal problem-solving beyond single-repository patching. FRAMES [27] contains 824 challenging multi-hop questions whose answers require combining information from two to fifteen Wikipedia articles. In our agentic formulation, the model searches fixed Wikipedia corpus, opens relevant articles incrementally, and submits free-form answer evaluated against the reference answer by an LM judge. The benchmark consequently tests iterative retrieval and evidence integration while allowing the retrieved evidence to accumulate in the interaction history. 𝜏 2-bench [7] evaluates agents that converse with simulated user while operating domain-specific tools under explicit policy constraints. We use the 184-task golden set spanning retail, airline, and telecommunications; success requires both satisfying the users request and bringing the environment to the correct final state. Its mixture of dialogue, reasoning, and state-changing tool calls tests whether information established early in an interaction remains usable by later actions. BFCLv3 [36] evaluates multi-turn tool use in simulated environments. We use its 200 long-context episodes, which require agents to retain information across user turns and schedule state-changing tool 4 You dont need long context calls. Long-input task benchmarks. The long-input task benchmark group holds the task question comparatively short while making the information needed to answer it large, at least in principle. It includes three broad, realistic long-document QA benchmarks and four needle-style benchmarks. LongBench v2 [6] comprises 503 challenging multiple-choice questions with heterogeneous, predominantly natural inputs ranging from 8K to approximately 2M words. Its six task families cover singleand multi-document question answering, long in-context learning, long dialogue, code-repository understanding, and structured-data understanding. LOONG [45] is 1,600-question multi-document benchmark in which question typically depends on multiple complete financial reports, legal cases, or academic papers in either English or Chinese. Its locating, comparison, clustering, and chain-of-reasoning tasks are designed so that evidence is distributed across multiple load-bearing documents. Artificial Analysis Long Context Reasoning (AA-LCR) [4] comprises 100 human-crafted questions requiring reasoning across sets of real-world documents averaging approximately 100K input tokens. Its seven document categories include company and industry reports, government consultations, academic and legal documents, marketing materials, and survey reports. Answers require integrating evidence and performing multi-step reasoning across documents, rather than retrieving directly stated fact. Needle in Haystack (NIAH) [24] consists of target sentences inserted at controlled depths in long bodies of unrelated essay text and of asking for the fact expressed by that sentence. Our 125-instance grid varies both insertion depth and document length, with contexts extending from 16K to roughly 500K tokens. RULER [22] is synthetic long-context suite containing thirteen tasks: eight needle-retrieval variants, variable tracking, commonand frequent-word extraction, and two multi-hop question-answering tasks. We evaluate all thirteen at 256K and 500K tokens and score the recall of the required answer set. Counting-Stars [39] scatters 32 marked numbers throughout long text and asks the model to recover them all. We use the complete 192-question public set, spanning English and Chinese, acquisition and reasoning variants, and documents from 4K to 128K tokens. The reasoning variant includes initially incorrect counts that are subsequently corrected, requiring the model to distinguish the final value from nearby distractor rather than merely copy every marked number. BABILong [28] consists of short facts from the bAbI [46] reasoning tasks embedded into book text. Answering requires locating the relevant statements and then performing operations such as fact chaining, counting, negation, or set tracking. We evaluate 550 questions across all ten task types and five input lengths from 64K to 1M tokens. Note that even the needle-style benchmarks considered often do not feature clear lexical overlap aiding easy retrieval. They do, however, require aggregation, variable tracking, or reasoning over multiple retrieved facts for the correct answer to be produced. 2.3. Models We perform our study on two groups of models. Large closed-weight models are used as the workers in our principal task-accuracy experiments, while large open-weight models support the cloud system throughput study and complementary local experiments. Large closed-weight models. Our principal benchmark experiments use Claude Opus 4.5 and GPT 5.6 Sol. We select these models as representative of the strong general-purpose models used for coding, tool use, and other long-horizon workflows. Using independently developed model families also reduces the risk that an observed effect of compaction is specific to one provider or post-training recipe. Large open-weight models. We use large open-weight models for two additional parts of the experimentation. First, the cloud-throughput study in Figure 1 uses models large enough to require multi-GPU deployment and exposes the effect of context window size under saturated serving load: GLM 5.2 [17, 50], evaluated at context window sizes up to 1M tokens; Kimi K2.6 [32], evaluated at context window sizes up to 256K tokens; and 5 You dont need long context Qwen 3 Coder Next [9], evaluated at context window sizes up to 256K tokens. We fit the context-cost ratio from these throughput measurements and define the RQ1 optimized-retail-cost estimate in Appendix B. Second, we use locally deployable open-weight models for the on-device systems measurements in Figure 2 and for complementary task-level experiments. We deploy them on an NVIDIA DGX Spark [33], whose 128GB of unified memory leaves about 109GB available for local LM serving. Such deployments are relevant when source code or other task data must remain on-device for privacy or cost reasons. The two Qwen checkpoints are served in NVFP4 [1]; the remaining three are served from GGUF weights through llama.cpp using 3to 4-bit k-/i-quantization. Together they cover hybrid linear/softmax attention, distinct interleaved sliding-window/global-attention stacks, gated grouped-query attention, and conventional full grouped-query softmax attention. This architectural diversity helps to test the sufficiency of short context claimed in RQ1 across models with different attention mechanisms and post-training characteristics. Qwen 3.6 27B [37] is 27B-parameter dense model served in NVFP4. Its layers alternate in 3:1 pattern between Gated DeltaNet and gated full attention. It has context window size of 256K tokens. Qwen 3 Coder Next [9] is sparse MoE model with 80B total and 3B active parameters, served in NVFP4. It uses the same hybrid Gated DeltaNet/full-attention pattern and has context window size of 256K tokens. Gemma 4 31B [16] is 31B-parameter dense model served from GGUF Q4_K_M weights. It interleaves 1024-token local sliding-window attention with global-attention layers and has context window size of 256K tokens. Step 3.7 Flash (198B A11B) [40] is sparse MoE model with 198B total and 11B active parameters, served from GGUF Q3_K_M weights. It interleaves 512-token sliding-window and full-attention layers in 3:1 pattern, uses head-wise gated grouped-query attention, and has context window size of 256K tokens. MiniMax M2.7 [10] is sparse MoE model with 230B total and 10B active parameters, served from GGUF IQ3_XXS weights. It uses full-softmax grouped-query attention throughout and has context window size of 200K tokens [31]. 2.4. Harnesses We use two closely related base harnesses. Both implement minimal ReAct loop: the task is supplied in an initial user message, the model issues one Bash action at time, and each action and its result are appended to the conversation [49]. When used, the Bash environment exposes the files, programs, and benchmark-specific utilities available to the agent. Each Bash invocation treats the related standard output, return code, and any execution error as action results. mini-swe-agent. For software-engineering and terminal tasks, we use the released mini-swe-agent harness [41], with only the environment integration required by each benchmark. Its system prompt describes the software-engineering workflow, and its Bash environment provides the task repository or container. When done, the agent submits its proposed pull request as patch for evaluation. mini-agent. For the remaining benchmarks, we use our mini-agent harness, which is straightforward generalization of mini-swe-agent away from software engineering. It retains the same agent loop, model interface, and Bash interface, but uses benchmark-specific instructions, environments, and submission rules. The instructions specify the available commands, task procedure, and required answer format. Only the system instruction and task description are provided in the initial user message. Supporting inputs and tools are made available through the environment. When done, an evaluation benchmark adapter recognizes the designated submission command, extracts its payload, terminates the episode, and records the prediction in the benchmark evaluators required format. 2.4.1. Accommodations for long conversational context We compare three context-management regimes applied to the base harnesses described above. These regimes determine which interaction history is presented to the model. The regimes functioning is illustrated in 6 You dont need long context Figure 3. Figure 3 Context-management regimes. The three context-management regimes considered in this work: Full-History Accumulation (FHA), End-of-Conversation Compaction (EoCC), and Single-Action Compaction (SAC). Full-History Accumulation (FHA). The baseline full-history accumulation regime appends every model action and environment observation to single conversation for the duration of the task. No history is removed or replaced during run. This is the default mode of operation for mini-swe-agent and mini-agent. End-of-Conversation Compaction (EoCC). This regime follows the full-history ReAct loop until the length of the conversational context crosses pre-specified compaction threshold. The model is then instructed within the active conversation to produce bounded, task-relevant compaction of its state (see Appendix A). higher total context limit reserves space for this compaction turn and terminates the conversation if compaction does not complete in time. The harness starts fresh conversation containing the original task and the compacted state, and execution resumes under the same system prompt. This cycle repeats whenever the compaction threshold is crossed. We write these two values as total context limit / compaction threshold in tokens. Single-Action Compaction (SAC). This regime maintains compact semantic state and essentially no conversational history. Each conversation receives the task and current semantic state, performs exactly one environment action, observes its result, and updates the semantic state. The harness then discards that conversation and starts fresh one for the next action. For the experiments in Section 5, we apply SAC as context-management regime to mini-swe-agent; the underlying agent harness, model, and task environment otherwise remain unchanged. SAC therefore keeps the active conversational context shortest of the three regimes and operationalizes the single-action setting of RQ3. Context length measures. We distinguish total length from peak length. For full-history baseline, total length is the length of its executions conversation. For EoCC and SAC, total length is the sum of the final lengths of all conversations created during the execution. Peak length is the length of the largest conversation produced during the task. Both measures are expressed in thousands of tokens (K) and summarized across tasks as mean / median / maximum or median / maximum, as indicated in each table. 2.4.2. Accommodations for long inputs We enable selective input reading by storing each long input as one or more documents (e.g., input01.txt, input02.txt) in the agents filesystem environment rather than placing their full contents in the initial conversation. The task message identifies the available documents, and the agent performs selective input reading using standard Bash tools (e.g., sed, awk, head). This method of input presentation makes selective input reading an explicit environment action and thereby reduces long-input workload to long-horizon workload. We provide the agent instructions and examples of selective reading in Appendix E. 7 You dont need long context Figure 4 Decode throughput collapses as the context window size grows. Peak sustained decode throughput (tokens/s, left axis) for open-weight coding models served under vLLM on NVIDIA H100 GPUs, as function of the configured context window size. GLM 5.2 and Kimi K2.6 are served with INT4 experts and BF16 activations (Kimi additionally with an FP8 KV cache), Qwen 3 Coder Next in BF16. The right axis re-expresses the same curve as speedup over the 256K operating point. Reducing the context window size from 256K to 16K buys 3.6 (GLM 5.2), 5.6 (Kimi K2.6), and 7 (Qwen 3 Coder Next) more decoded tokens per second on identical hardware. 2.5. Latency and throughput measurement Cloud serving. For each model, we use the smallest H100 node-deployment that can hold the served checkpoint and KV cache at the maximum evaluated context window size: eight H100 GPUs for Qwen 3 Coder Next and sixteen for GLM 5.2 and Kimi K2.6. For each context window size, we draw request lengths uniformly from nested prefixes of shared token sequence, with sufficient space reserved for generation. We prefill the longest prefix once, enable prefix caching, and require every subsequent prefix request to generate exactly 1, 024 tokens. After warm-up, we sweep request concurrency and measure sustained aggregate decode throughput as completed output tokens divided by elapsed time. We report the highest-throughput setting with no KV-cache preemption; repeated measurements varied by at most 2%. The results are in Figure 4. The cost values in Figure 1 convert these throughput measurements to the cost of 1M output tokens using the stated hourly GPU price. Local serving. On the DGX Spark, we evaluate one model instance and one request at time. For each model, we construct sequence at its maximum supported length and measure generation after prefixes of increasing length drawn from that sequence. At each length, we record the mean inter-token latency over the next 1, 024 generated tokens and the total device-memory consumption. The batch-one decode throughput in Figure 2 is the reciprocal of the mean inter-token latency. 8 You dont need long context 3. Long-horizon tasks dont need long contexts RQ1. Can long-horizon tasks be completed without long contexts? Answer: Yes. Frequent compaction keeps the context short while broadly maintaining task accuracy. Following the outline of Section 2, we evaluate EoCC on 6 benchmarks representing long-horizon workloads and measure the performance of EoCC-modified harnesses against their baseline FHA counterparts. For each benchmark and model, we sequentially decrease the total context token limit and the corresponding compaction threshold to fit the total context limit. This has the effect of lowering the maximum context window needed by the model and of triggering increasingly more frequent compactions while executing long-horizon tasks. We describe what these compactions are designed to preserve in Appendix A. For SWE-bench Verified, TerminalBench 2.1, SWE-bench Multilingual, and FRAMES, we evaluate the models at total context limits / compaction thresholds (cf. Section 2.4.1) of 48K/36K, 32K/24K, 24K/18K, and 16K/12K. For BFCLv3, we consider 24K/18K, 16K/12K, and 12K/8K, while for Tau2Bench, we consider 16K/12K, 12K/8K, and 8K/6K. Figure 5 plots the EoCC accuracies and estimated cost savings relative to FHA baselines against increasing levels of compaction. Figure 5 Long-horizon results as function of total context limit. Top: accuracy changes in percentage points relative to each models full-history baseline; zero indicates unchanged accuracy. Bottom: baseline estimated optimized retail cost divided by the compaction configurations estimated optimized retail cost; 1 indicates unchanged cost. Orange/blue identify Claude Opus 4.5 and GPT 5.6 Sol, respectively, and stars mark the baselines. Cost estimates use the model in Appendix B. 9 You dont need long context Skimming through the line plots, observe first that the performance broadly remains flat, sometimes falling few points below, sometimes remaining elevated above the baseline. More specifically, across all benchmarks and compaction thresholds, the relative performance of Opus 4.5 ranges from -3.7 to +5.6ppts, while the relative performance of GPT 5.6 Sol ranges from -3.3 to +4.4. The ranges are somewhat deceiving when considered by themselves, however: for either model, no more than 5 out of 22 threshold configurations lose more than 2ppts of the baseline. Secondly, observe the multiples of cost savings across all benchmarks, ranging from 2.2x to 8.8x for Opus 4.5 and from 2.4x to 5.0x for GPT 5.6 Sol. These represent the estimated cost savings as consequence of serving only shorter context window sizes, and are considerable. One pathology that could occur due to frequent compaction is that while it may successfully enforce smaller context window size, the full workflow history might be becoming longer as consequence of the model having to re-do previously done tasks or to revisit previously seen information. Such behavior could result in an increased total token spend per task, ultimately erasing some of the cost savings due to smaller context windows. In our experimentation, this was generally not the case. Detailed per-benchmark accuracy, token spend, total length, cost and their discussion are provided in Appendix C. In sum, we observe that even the naive approach to keeping context short by compacting agents work history once its conversation reaches certain restrictive threshold leads to, broadly-speaking, on-par performance in model performance on long-horizon tasks when using frontier closed-weight models. Complementary results for open-weight models are provided in Appendix D. It would seem that the benefits of maintaining long contexts manifest themselves inconsistently and are not drastic so as to discourage efforts to keep the working context short in autonomous agentic workloads. Hence our answer to RQ1: yes. 3.1. Long-horizon tasks may sometimes need the history Long-horizon tasks may sometimes need the history, but that does not mean that they require long contexts. Compaction is lossy context compression method. Information will be lost as consequence of compacting conversational history. Even more information will be lost if the conversational history being compacted already contains result of an earlier compaction. It is not too difficult to construct task whose accuracy is guaranteed to suffer when compaction is performed. Consider, for example, an agent that has access to tool that generates coin tosses and reports the outcome of each coin toss in its tool result. With compaction budget fixed, the agent is guaranteed to eventually start losing information about the outcomes of some of the coin tosses. If, at some point, the agent needs to inspect the sequence of coin toss outcomes (e.g., access the 𝑖th outcome), it is guaranteed to eventually fail as consequence of some compaction necessarily eliminating some of its toss outcome records, with the compaction being the cause. Observe, however, that any such example can be eliminated by creating harness that keeps record of every message of any agentic conversation, and makes it readily accessible to the agent by the means of selective reading tool. The querying of the agents conversational history then becomes long-input task, which we tackle in RQ2. In other words, there is difference between information that needs to be part of model context and information that could, in principle, be retrieved selectively on need-to-know basis. Note that the findings of our experimentation above are not that you dont ever need to access conversational history, but roughly that you dont need to keep the entire conversational history in the context in order to complete long-horizon tasks. 10 You dont need long context 4. Long-input tasks dont need long contexts RQ2. Can long-input tasks be completed without long contexts? Answer: Yes. Selective input reading and compaction keep contexts short, maintaining task accuracy. We evaluate EoCC on 7 benchmarks representing long-input workloads and measure the performance of EoCC-modified harnesses against their baseline full-input counterparts. For each benchmark and model, the full-input baseline receives the entirety of the input as prescribed by the benchmark while the compacting harness uses Bash tools to perform selective reading of inputs from environment filesystem (see Appendix E). Where appropriate in EoCC runs, we further sequentially decrease the total context token limit and the corresponding compaction threshold to fit the total context limit. For many long-input tasks (especially the needle-based tasks), one restrictive total token limit is enough to showcase on-par or better performance. Figure 6 plots the EoCC accuracies and estimated cost savings relative to FHA baselines against one or multiple levels of compaction. Figure 6 Long-input results as function of total context limit. Top: accuracy changes relative to each models full-input baseline. Bottom: optimized retail cost savings, using the model in Appendix B. You dont need long context Looking through the line plots, observe first that the performance broadly remains flat, sometimes falling few points below, sometimes remaining elevated above the baseline. More specifically, across all benchmarks and compaction thresholds, the relative performance of Opus 4.5 ranges from -0.4 to +40.0ppts, while the relative performance of GPT 5.6 Sol ranges from +1.0 to +30.9 (!). Observe also the multiples of cost savings across all benchmarks, ranging from 6.5x to 54.6x for Opus 4.5 and from 4.4x to 233.3x for GPT 5.6 Sol. These represent the estimated cost savings as consequence of both selective input reading and serving only shorter context window sizes, and warrant serious consideration. Figures 7 and 8 plot total conversation length, summed across stretches, against document length. On logarithmic document-length axes spanning orders of magnitude, conversation lengths on the linear vertical axes remain concentrated in broadly similar bands for most tasks, with some longer outliers. The dashed equal-length reference 𝑦 = 𝑥 rises exponentially in these plotting coordinates, whereas most conversations do not grow proportionally with document length. This shows that even as document length increases, the conversation length remains broadly bounded. Figure 7 LongBench v2: conversation length versus document length. Claude Opus 4.5, compaction at 16K / 12K. The document-length axis is logarithmic and the conversation-length axis is linear. The dashed curve marks 𝑦 = 𝑥. 12 You dont need long context Figure 8 LOONG: conversation length versus document length. Claude Opus 4.5, compaction at 48K / 40K (1,600 questions). The document-length axis is logarithmic and the conversation-length axis is linear. The dashed curve marks 𝑦 = 𝑥. The near-zero median number of compactions and the roughly constant conversation lengths as document size grows support the intuition that despite the long inputs provided to tasks, the actual amount of information required to solve those tasks remains low. Thus, the size of tasks input does not itself establish need for long context. Hence our answer to RQ2: yes. 13 You dont need long context 5. Compaction can be performed after every action RQ3. Can long-horizon tasks be completed taking no more than single action per context? Answer: Yes. Single-action compaction maintains an effective compact semantic state. This is somewhat remarkable, considering that both models reduce each interaction to single action and carry only compact semantic state between contexts. The resulting live contexts are far shorter than the full-history conversations, showing that compaction frequency can be pushed to relative extremes without catastrophic consequences for task accuracy. Hence our answer to RQ3: yes. 5.1. Semantic State Space Models (SSSMs). The above observations of Section 5 and earlier observations of Sections 3 and 4 force reflection: If powerful models can broadly maintain performance by compacting often or even compacting after taking single action, cannot all long-context workflows be coerced into becoming single-action workflows through compaction? In other words, could not all models potentially be performing single-action compaction (SAC) by default? To do so would roughly correspond to maintaining semantic state across long-context workflows. We propose the notion of Semantic State Space Model (SSSM). SSSM is model post-trained to (1) comprehend an input language description of state of conversation, (2) reason about the appropriate next action or about the task at hand, (3) take an action, (4) register its outcome, and (5) update the language description of the conversations state with the reasoning conclusions, action decisions, and action outcomes in way that allows separate inference instance of the SSSM to continue the conversation toward completion. The notion of SSSM is closely related to that of State-Space Model [19, 20, 18]. Unlike an SSM, which maintains black-box neural state between token generations, an SSSM maintains an explainable natural language (hence semantic) state between turns of continuing conversation. The utility of SSSMs as opposed to existing conversational models trained for growing full-history conversations lies in their increased token efficiency as shown in Figure 1, there is considerable cost benefit to maintaining short contexts. We further surmise that it is considerably more data-efficient to train semantic state-space 14 You dont need long context models due to the lack of need to teach the model to pay attention to the suitable patches of earlier context. Ultimately, we see no reason why SSSMs could not match the performance of full-history-accumulating models, which begs the question: Why train full-history-accumulating models in the first place? 6. Conclusion Our experiments provide affirmative answers to all three research questions RQ1RQ3. In particular, we found that on long-horizon tasks, even simple end-of-conversation compaction usually matches or slightly improves on full-history accuracy, with only modest losses in the remaining settings. We showed that on long-input tasks, selective input reading with compaction as fallback matches or improves (sometimes considerably) the full-input baselines in almost every case while keeping live context short. Finally, single-action compaction nearly preserves or improves on the baseline accuracy while carrying only compact semantic state between actions. RQ1RQ3 were motivated by the root question RQ0: Are long contexts necessary? Based on the affirmative answers to all of the above, we conclude that long contexts are not necessary for the completion of long-context tasks. This is far from surprising. After all, the very motivation behind the definition of computability rests on the assumption that anything computable may be computed by comprehending only bounded amount of input at time and maintaining only finite state of mind [44]. Our evidence does not rule out the existence of tasks for which long context is beneficial, nor does it prove that every possible task can be solved with short context. It does, however, show that the standard arguments in favor of long contexts stemming from long input and long conversational horizons are insufficient: disciplined state maintenance and selective access remove the presumed necessity in every setting we tested. We believe that with the appropriate adjustments made to the post-training of LMs, the context window size requirements currently imposed on these models by the standard arguments for long contexts could be removed, and model context window sizes could shrink drastically, significantly improving the cost of token generation on the cloud and the speed of token generation on local inference accelerators.

What characterizes good compaction? It is common experience of human-in-the-loop agent-aided SWE workflows that after compaction is performed, certain crucial information disappears from the context and has to be obtained again, slowing down the SWE process or perhaps even confusing the model and losing crucial user preferences included in previous instructions. Note that human-in-the-loop agent-aided SWE workflows consist of two parts: autonomous SWE work performed by the agent, and reception and comprehension of the humans steering feedback. Because of this, compactions produced for such workflows need to account for not only the information the agent needs to achieve its goals, but also for all potential information that might be relevant to follow-up autonomous work that might be triggered as result of the humans feedback. In our experimentation, we initially set out to identify the cheapest, most useful method of compaction that can preserve as much task accuracy as possible on autonomous SWE work. We discovered that treating compaction as mere special case of summarization is suboptimal for this purpose. LM summarizations generally attempt to give equal weight to all facts present in the input and are prone to overemphasize repeated segments of the agent trace regardless of their ultimate relevance to the tail of the trace being compacted. We explored the subject along two axes: the method (e.g., summarization or message pruning) and the information being pruned (e.g., the entire trace or only the trace segment since the last compaction plus the contents of the last compaction). We discovered that the best compactions are not those that faithfully capture the gist of the agentic trace, but those that best select facts relevant to the work yet to be performed i.e., they are not narratives of the execution history but carefully cherry-picked briefs for further execution. In particular, we found that the most accuracy-preserving compactions, regardless of the frequency of compaction, are those that contain (1) verbatim or near-verbatim copy of the input task, (2) record of agents current occupation, intentions, and planned next steps, and (3) all the artifacts that are of direct relevance to future execution, including (3a) decomposed plan made from the input task, (3b) list of requirements detailing when to consider the task complete, and any pieces of information or pointers to artifacts containing information that is of relevance to the aforementioned two. Finally, we found that the above structure of compactions readily extends even to workflows that are not necessarily SWE-related in their nature. Selective reading of long inputs Our generalized adaptation of mini-swe-agent, mini-agent, exposes long benchmark inputs as text files that the agent can inspect through bash tool. LongBench v2 uses one document file, whereas LOONG and AA-LCR expose multiple source files. The operation of mini-agent is straightforward. The model receives the question and file information and then chooses which text to retrieve in order to start answering the question. succession of Bash-invoked searches then scan entire files, but only their returned matched excerpts enter the models context. The basic process of single search is to identify the entities, quantities, or claims needed for the answer, and then to read small surrounding window to interpret the candidate evidence. Further related searches might then be used to retrieve more candidates looked up using broader sets of synonyms. Standard commands such as grep, sed, head, and tail are the backbone of the search process. Convenience commands provide document sizes (doc-stats), file manifests (docs-list), bounded reads (doc-read), and search-term variants (doc-syn) allow for more surgical readouts from files and expanded search follow-ups. E.1. Instructions supplied to the agent. The base system prompt gives the following man-like tool description: doc-read [--start CHAR] [--chars N] [--lines A:B] Read BOUNDED window (default 6000 chars, hard-capped at 8000). Give character offset window, or 1-based inclusive line range. The header tells you the command to read the next contiguous window. This is how you read the document sequentially without ever exceeding your budget. grep -n -i -E <regex> "$LONGBENCH_DOC" Find where name / number / phrase appears (with -n for line numbers). Then doc-read around those lines. This is usually far faster than reading straight through -- locate the relevant passages, then read only those. ... The system prompt also makes the preference for selective reading explicit: IMPORTANT --- read only what you need. Keep each read small (<= 6000 chars). Do NOT try to dump the whole document. Search for the entities/claims each option hinges on, read the surrounding passages, and verify. E.2. Examples from recorded runs.
